A_target.statement:
[[Definition:Euler's Number|Euler's number]] $e$ is [[Definition:Transcendental Number|transcendental]].
That is, $e$ is not a root of any non-zero [[Definition:Polynomial over Ring|polynomial]] with [[Definition:Rational Number|rational]] coefficients.

B_source.statement:
To show a relation cannot hold, assume it and construct a quantity $N$ which is simultaneously an [[Definition:Integer|integer]] and satisfies:
:$0 < \size N < 1$
a contradiction.

substitutions.the assumed algebraic relation: a supposed integer polynomial relation satisfied by e
substitutions.the auxiliary quantity built from it: a combination of integrals of a carefully chosen polynomial times the exponential
substitutions.the two competing estimates: an integrality argument and an analytic size bound

derived.the quantity is a nonzero integer: divisibility forces it to be a nonzero multiple of a factorial
derived.the quantity is smaller than one: the analytic bound decays faster than the factorial grows

object_map.reformulation: Convert the algebraic assumption into a single number, then squeeze it between two incompatible estimates.

validity_conditions: The auxiliary polynomial must be chosen so that repeated differentiation produces coefficients divisible by a large factorial, which is what forces integrality.
The same choice must keep the analytic estimate small, so the polynomial degree is tuned to make the growth of the bound lose to the factorial.
The contradiction is that no integer lies strictly between zero and one; the entire construction exists only to produce one quantity satisfying both estimates.
proof_plan:
{{AimForCont}} that:
:$a_0 + a_1 e + \cdots + a_n e^n = 0$
with $a_i \in \Z$ and $a_0 \ne 0$.

For a prime $p$, let $\map f x = \dfrac {x^{p - 1} \paren {x - 1}^p \cdots \paren {x - n}^p} {\paren {p - 1}!}$ and:
:$\displaystyle \map I t = \int_0^t e^{t - x} \map f x \rd x$
Form $N = \displaystyle \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \map I k$.

By repeated [[Integration by Parts]], $\map I t = e^t \map F 0 - \map F t$ with $F = \displaystyle \sum_j f^{\paren j}$.
Using the assumed relation, $N = -\displaystyle \sum_k a_k \map F k$.
Each $\map {f^{\paren j} } k$ is an integer divisible by $p$, except $\map {f^{\paren {p - 1} } } 0 = \paren {\paren {-1}^n n!}^p$.
For $p > \max \set {n, \size {a_0} }$, $N$ is a non-zero integer.

But $\size {\map I k} \le k e^k \max_{\closedint 0 n} \size f \le C^p / \paren {p - 1}!$ for a constant $C$.
Hence $\size N < 1$ for $p$ large, a contradiction.
This is the [[Hermite-Lindemann-Weierstrass Theorem|transcendence of $e$]].
{{qed}}
